rows.speaker: عبد الله بن شبرمة
rows.claim: Ibn Shibrima reasoned that because no sura has fewer than three verses, one should not recite fewer than three verses.
rows.anchor: نظرت كم يكفي الرجل من القرآن فلم أجد سورة أقل من ثلاث آيات

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet said that reciting the last two verses of al-Baqara at night suffices the reciter; Ibn Kathir says this report is agreed upon by al-Bukhari and Muslim.
rows.anchor: فذكر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أن من قرأ بالآيتين من آخر سورة البقرة في ليلة كفتاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says al-Bukhari’s joined transmission is sound: Abd al-Rahman first heard it from Alqama, then directly from Abu Masud while circumambulating the Kaaba; Ali is Ibn al-Madini and his teacher Sufyan ibn Uyayna.
rows.anchor: عبد الرحمن سمعه أولا من علقمة، ثم لقي أبا مسعود وهو يطوف فسمعه منه

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن شبرمة
rows.claim: Ibn Shibrima was the leading jurist of Kufa in his time, and Ibn Kathir calls his inference a good one.
rows.anchor: وما قاله عبد الله بن شبرمة -فقيه الكوفة في زمانه-استنباط حسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Sunan report says prayer requires the Opening and three verses; Ibn Kathir judges the Abu Masud report more authentic, famous, and specific, while finding its fit with al-Bukhari’s chapter heading questionable.
rows.anchor: لا صلاة إلا بفاتحة الكتاب وثلاث آيات

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In the clearer report for the chapter heading, the Prophet counsels Abdullah ibn Amr, who fasted daily and completed the Quran nightly, to read it over a month, then weekly, and settle on the fast of David.
rows.anchor: فلما طال ذلك عليه ذكر للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، فقال: " "القني به"

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: After growing old and weak, Abdullah regretted not accepting the Prophet’s concession; he maintained his Quran and fasting routine by reciting a seventh by day and making up fasts.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد، عن عبد الله بن عمرو قال: أنكحني أبي امرأة ذات حسب، فكان يتعاهد كنته

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The report adds that some recited the Quran every three or five days, while most followed a seven-day completion.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: في ثلاث وفي خمس وأكثرهم على سبع

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: The Prophet told Abdullah to read the Quran in a month, then in seven days and not less; Ibn Kathir says this wording apparently bars a completion in fewer than seven days.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عمرو قال: " قال لي النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: "اقرأ القرآن في شهر"

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: When Qays ibn Sasaa asked how quickly to read, the Prophet first said every fifteen days, then allowed a weekly completion when Qays said he could do more.
rows.anchor: أنه قال للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: " يا رسول الله، في كم أقرأ القرآن؟ فقال: "في كل خمس عشرة"

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Abdullah ibn Masud used to complete the Quran from one Friday to the next outside Ramadan.
rows.anchor: كان عبد الله بن مسعود يقرأ القرآن في غير رمضان من الجمعة إلى الجمعة

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubay ibn Kaab used to complete the Quran every eight days.
rows.anchor: عن أبي المهلب قال: كان أبي بن كعب يختم القرآن في كل ثمان

rows.speaker: تميم الداري
rows.claim: Tamim al-Dari used to complete the Quran every seven days.
rows.anchor: وكان تميم الداري يختمه في كل سبع

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: Ibrahim al-Nakha‘i used to complete the Quran every seven days.
rows.anchor: عن الأعمش، عن إبراهيم: أنه كان يختم القرآن في كل سبع

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: Ibrahim reports that al-Aswad completed the Quran every six days and Alqama every five days.
rows.anchor: عن منصور، عن إبراهيم قال: كان الأسود يختم القرآن في كل ست

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taken alone, reports limiting completion to seven days would make the matter clear, but other reports establish that completing it sooner is permissible.
rows.anchor: ولكن دلت أحاديث أخرجوها (4) على جواز قراءته فيما دون ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir grades Ahmad’s chain for Saad ibn Mundhir’s report good, strong, and hasan: Hasan ibn Musa is reliable, Ibn Lahia explicitly heard it, and the other named transmitters are trusted.
rows.anchor: وهذا إسناد جيد قوي حسن، فإن حسن بن موسى الأشيب ثقة متفق على جلالته

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Saad ibn Mundhir asked whether he could read the Quran in three days; the Prophet answered yes, adding in Abu Ubayd’s version, if he was able, and Saad kept to it until death.
rows.anchor: عن سعد بن المنذر الأنصاري أنه قال: " يا رسول الله، أقرأ القرآن في ثلاث؟ قال: "نعم، إن استطعت"

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet said that one who completes the Quran in fewer than three days does not understand it; al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan sahih.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: " لا يفقه من قرأه في أقل من ثلاث "

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A report from Aisha says the Prophet never completed the Quran in fewer than three days; Ibn Kathir calls it unusual and weak because al-Tayyib ibn Sulayman was weakened by al-Daraqutni and was little known.
rows.anchor: أنها سمعت عائشة تقول: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يختم القرآن في أقل من ثلاث

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: A number of early and later authorities, including Abu Ubayd, Ishaq, and Ibn Rahawayh, disliked completing the Quran in less than three days; Ibn Kathir says the report from Muadh is sound.
rows.anchor: عن معاذ بن جبل أنه كان يكره أن يقرأ القرآن في أقل من ثلاث

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abdullah ibn Masud said that whoever reads the Quran in fewer than three days is a rajiz, a hurried or metrical reciter.
rows.anchor: عبد الله: من قرأ القرآن في أقل من ثلاث فهو راجز

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Abdullah ibn Masud used to complete the Quran in three days during Ramadan; Ibn Kathir grades this report’s chain sound.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الرحمن بن عبد الله بن مسعود، عن أبيه؛ أنه كان يقرأ القرآن في رمضان في ثلاث

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن شبل
rows.claim: A report raised to the Prophet instructs readers to avoid excess and neglect, and not to earn from or amass wealth through the Quran.
rows.anchor: وفي المسند عن عبد الرحمن بن شبل مرفوعا: "اقرؤوا القرآن، ولا تغلوا فيه، ولا تجفوا عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir explains that excess means racing through recitation in the shortest time, which usually prevents reflection; neglect means abandoning recitation.
rows.anchor: لا تبالغوا في تلاوته بسرعة في أقصر مدة، فإن ذلك ينافي التدبر غالبا

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and his adherents hold that al-Fatiha is not specifically required in prayer; any Quran recitation suffices, based on the general wording of this verse.
rows.anchor: فعند أبي حنيفة ومن وافقه من أصحابه وغيرهم أنها لا تتعين، بل مهما قرأ به من القرآن أجزأه في الصلاة

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa’s side also cites the Prophet’s instruction to a man who prayed badly to recite whatever Quran was easy, without naming al-Fatiha.
rows.anchor: إذا قمت إلى الصلاة فكبر، ثم اقرأ ما تيسر معك من القرآن

rows.speaker: مالك والشافعي وأحمد بن حنبل
rows.claim: Malik, al-Shafii, Ahmad, their followers, and most scholars require al-Fatiha specifically and consider prayer without it invalid, citing reports that the prayer is deficient or invalid without it.
rows.anchor: وهو قول بقية الأئمة: مالك والشافعي وأحمد بن حنبل وأصحابهم وجمهور العلماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir explains khidaj in the report about omitting al-Fatiha as deficient, meaning not complete.
rows.anchor: والخداج هو: الناقص كما فسر به في الحديث: " غير تمام "

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Reports from Ubada ibn al-Samit and Abu Hurayra say there is no prayer without al-Fatiha or the Mother of the Quran; Ibn Kathir notes many reports on the issue.
rows.anchor: لا صلاة لمن لم يقرأ بفاتحة الكتاب

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafii and some scholars require al-Fatiha in every rakah.
rows.anchor: ثم إن مذهب الشافعي وجماعة من أهل العلم: أنه تجب قراءتها في كل ركعة.

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Other scholars say al-Fatiha is required in most rakahs rather than every rakah.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: إنما تجب قراءتها في معظم الركعات

rows.speaker: الحسن وأكثر البصريين
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and most Basrans hold that al-Fatiha is required in only one rakah, relying on the unrestricted hadith wording.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وأكثر البصريين: إنما تجب قراءتها في ركعة واحدة من الصلوات

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأصحابه والثوري والأوزاعي
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa, his adherents, al-Thawri, and al-Awzai hold that al-Fatiha is not specifically required and another passage suffices, citing this verse.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة وأصحابه والثوري والأوزاعي: لا تتعين (1) قراءتها، بل لو قرأ بغيرها أجزأه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Abu Said says prayer is not sufficient without al-Hamd and a sura in every rakah, whether obligatory or voluntary; Ibn Kathir questions its soundness.
rows.anchor: عن أبي سعيد مرفوعا: " لا صلاة لمن لم يقرأ في كل ركعة بالحمد وسورة في فريضة أو غيرها "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir sets out three views on whether a person praying behind an imam must recite al-Fatiha.
rows.anchor: هل تجب قراءة الفاتحة على المأموم؟ فيه ثلاثة أقوال للعلماء

rows.speaker: أحدها
rows.claim: The first view makes al-Fatiha obligatory for the follower just as it is for the imam, relying on the general hadiths already cited.
rows.anchor: أحدها: أنه تجب عليه قراءتها، كما تجب على إمامه

rows.speaker: الثاني
rows.claim: The second view requires no recitation by the follower in either quiet or audible prayer; Ibn Kathir says the prophetic chains for its proof are all unsound.
rows.anchor: والثاني: لا تجب على المأموم قراءة بالكلية لا الفاتحة ولا غيرها، لا في الصلاة الجهرية ولا السرية

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says that when someone has an imam, the imam’s recitation is his recitation; Ibn Kathir calls its chain weak and notes Malik reports it as Jabir’s own statement.
rows.anchor: " من كان له إمام فقراءة الإمام له قراءة " ولكن في إسناده ضعف

rows.speaker: القول الثالث
rows.claim: The third view requires the follower to recite in quiet prayers but not audible ones; Ibn Kathir says the evidence supports this position, an old view of al-Shafii and a report from Ahmad.
rows.anchor: والقول الثالث: أنه تجب القراءة على المأموم في السرية، لما (7) تقدم، ولا تجب (8) في الجهرية

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Reports from Abu Musa and Abu Hurayra instruct worshippers to listen silently when the imam recites; Muslim authenticated the report and Ibn Kathir uses it to support the third view.
rows.anchor: إنما جعل الإمام ليؤتم به؛ فإذا كبر فكبروا، وإذا قرأ فأنصتوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir raises these disputes to show that al-Fatiha has rulings not shared by the other suras.
rows.anchor: والغرض من ذكر هذه المسائل هاهنا بيان اختصاص سورة الفاتحة بأحكام لا تتعلق بغيرها من السور

words: وإن كنتم في ريب مما نزلنا على عبدنا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After establishing that God alone is deity, Ibn Kathir says the passage turns to establishing prophethood by addressing those who doubt what God revealed to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: ثم شرع تعالى في تقرير النبوة بعد أن قرر أنه (1) لا إله إلا هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge means that if doubters claim the revelation came from someone other than God, they should produce a comparable sura and seek whatever help they wish; they cannot do so.
rows.anchor: فإنكم لا تستطيعون ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes the called witnesses to mean helpers who could assist in meeting the challenge.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: {شهداءكم} أعوانكم [أي: قوما آخرين

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi, transmitting from Abu Malik, explains the witnesses as the polytheists’ partners or gods, whom they should enlist for support.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي، عن أبي مالك: شركاءكم [أي استعينوا بآلهتكم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the witnesses are people who can attest to the challenge, meaning eloquent judges.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: {وادعوا شهداءكم} قال: ناس يشهدون به [يعني: حكام الفصحاء]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeats the challenge elsewhere, asking for a better book, its like, ten comparable suras, or one sura; Ibn Kathir notes that all these earlier challenge verses are Meccan.
rows.anchor: وقد تحداهم الله تعالى بهذا في غير موضع من القرآن، فقال في سورة القصص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge was also made in Medina in this verse, after earlier Meccan challenges.
rows.anchor: ثم تحداهم [الله تعالى] (4) بذلك -أيضا-في المدينة،

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Mujahid and Qatada understand min mithlihi as a sura like the Quran; Ibn Jarir selects this reading.
rows.anchor: يعني: من مثل [هذا] (6) القرآن؛ قاله مجاهد وقتادة، واختاره ابن جرير.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir supports the Quran-referent reading by citing the commands to bring ten suras like it and the declaration that none can bring its like.
rows.anchor: بدليل قوله: {فأتوا بعشر سور مثله} [هود: 13] وقوله: {لا يأتون بمثله} [الإسراء: 88]

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some interpret the phrase as asking for a sura from a person like Muhammad, that is, another unlettered man; Ibn Kathir rejects this and prefers the Quran-referent reading because the challenge addresses all people.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: من مثل محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم، يعني: من رجل أمي مثله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir prefers taking the challenge as a demand for a Quran-like sura: it addresses everyone, including the most eloquent nation, and they failed despite repeated challenges and hostility.
rows.anchor: والصحيح الأول؛ لأن التحدي عام لهم كلهم، مع أنهم أفصح الأمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their failure and the prediction that they never will produce a match are a further miracle; the Quran has never been matched and cannot be, since creaturely speech cannot resemble God’s speech.
rows.anchor: وهذه -أيضا-معجزة أخرى، وهو أنه أخبر أن هذا القرآن لا يعارض بمثله أبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For those who understand Arabic, the Quran’s inimitability appears in both its wording and meaning; Ibn Kathir cites debate over whether its wording is perfected and meanings detailed, or vice versa.
rows.anchor: ومن تدبر القرآن وجد فيه من وجوه الإعجاز فنونا ظاهرة وخفية من حيث اللفظ ومن جهة المعنى،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir cites Hud 11:1 as describing the Quran’s verses as perfected and then explained, while noting disagreement over whether this describes wording or meanings.
rows.anchor: الر كتاب أحكمت آياته ثم فصلت من لدن حكيم خبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran’s language and meaning are both eloquent beyond comparison; its reports about past and future unseen matters came to pass exactly as stated.
rows.anchor: فكل من لفظه ومعناه فصيح لا يجارى ولا يدانى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir connects the Quran’s truthful reports and just rulings with 6:115, and contrasts them with exaggeration, lies, and invention in poetry.
rows.anchor: وتمت كلمة ربك صدقا وعدلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the Quran, long Arabic and other poetry often devotes most lines to women, horses, wine, praise, battles, or spectacles, with only a few worthwhile verses and much empty talk.
rows.anchor: كما قيل في الشعر: إن أعذبه أكذبه، وتجد القصيدة الطويلة المديدة قد استعمل غالبها في وصف النساء أو الخيل أو الخمر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran is eloquent at the highest level for those who know Arabic and its many modes of expression.
rows.anchor: وأما القرآن فجميعه فصيح في غاية نهايات البلاغة عند من يعرف ذلك تفصيلا وإجمالا ممن فهم كلام العرب وتصاريف التعبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran’s accounts remain sweet whether extended or concise, repeated or not; repetition increases its sweetness without wearing it out or tiring scholars.
rows.anchor: فإنه إن تأملت أخباره وجدتها في غاية الحلاوة، سواء كانت مبسوطة أو وجيزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its warnings can make mountains tremble, while its promises open hearts and make people long for paradise and nearness to the Merciful’s Throne.
rows.anchor: وإن أخذ في الوعيد والتهديد جاء منه ما تقشعر منه الجبال الصم الراسيات، فما ظنك بالقلوب الفاهمات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir illustrates the Quran’s promise with descriptions of hidden delights and paradise, and its warnings with threats of being swallowed by the earth or struck by a storm of stones.
rows.anchor: كما قال في الترغيب: {فلا تعلم نفس ما أخفي لهم من قرة أعين جزاء بما كانوا يعملون}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other examples depict punishment for wrongdoing and ask whether years of worldly enjoyment can help when the promised punishment arrives.
rows.anchor: وقال في الزجر: {فكلا أخذنا بذنبه}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Quranic verses set commands and prohibitions, they command good and beneficial things and forbid vile things.
rows.anchor: اشتملت على الأمر بكل معروف حسن نافع طيب محبوب، والنهي عن كل قبيح رذيل دنيء

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud and other early authorities say listeners should pay close attention whenever they hear God address the believers, because what follows is a command or prohibition.
rows.anchor: كما قال ابن مسعود وغيره من السلف: إذا سمعت الله تعالى يقول في القرآن {يا أيها الذين آمنوا} فأوعها سمعك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir cites 7:157 as summarizing the Quran’s commands: enjoining right, forbidding wrong, permitting good things, forbidding foul things, and lifting burdens.
rows.anchor: يأمرهم بالمعروف وينهاهم عن المنكر ويحل لهم الطيبات ويحرم عليهم الخبائث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Descriptions of the resurrection, paradise, and hell warn and encourage, call to good and away from evil, reduce attachment to worldly life, and guide people to God’s straight path and sound law.
rows.anchor: بشرت به وحذرت وأنذرت؛ ودعت إلى فعل الخيرات واجتناب المنكرات، وزهدت في الدنيا ورغبت في الأخرى

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet said every prophet received signs by which people could believe, while his distinctive sign was revelation from God, and he hoped to have the most followers on Judgment Day; Muslim gives this wording.
rows.anchor: ولهذا ثبت في الصحيحين عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، قال: "ما من نبي من الأنبياء إلا قد أعطي من الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir explains that the revelation specially given to Muhammad is the Quran, a miracle humans cannot match; many scholars do not regard the other revealed books as miraculous in this sense.
rows.anchor: إنما كان الذي أوتيته وحيا أوحاه الله إلي

rows.speaker: بعض المتكلمين
rows.claim: Some theologians argue that either the Quran itself exceeds human ability, or its opponents could have matched it but God diverted them; either way it is divine.
rows.anchor: إن كان هذا القرآن معجزا في نفسه لا يستطيع البشر الإتيان بمثله ولا في قواهم معارضته، فقد حصل المدعى وهو المطلوب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir rejects the diversion argument as the Quran’s true explanation because the Quran is inherently inimitable, but accepts it for concessive debate; Fakhr al-Din used it to address short suras such as al-Asr and al-Kawthar.
rows.anchor: وهذه الطريقة وإن لم تكن مرضية لأن القرآن في نفسه معجز لا يستطيع البشر معارضته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waqud, with fatHa on the waw, means fuel thrown into a fire to kindle it, such as firewood.
rows.anchor: أما الوقود، بفتح الواو، فهو ما يلقى في النار لإضرامها كالحطب ونحوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir links the fire’s fuel imagery to 72:15, where the unjust are firewood for Hell, and 21:98, where worshippers and their idols are fuel for it.
rows.anchor: كما قال: {وأما القاسطون فكانوا لجهنم حطبا} [الجن: 15] وقال تعالى: {إنكم وما تعبدون من دون الله حصب جهنم أنتم لها واردون}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir identifies the stones as enormous, black, hard, foul-smelling sulfur stones, among the hottest stones when heated.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالحجارة هاهنا: هي حجارة الكبريت العظيمة السوداء الصلبة المنتنة، وهي أشد الأحجار حرا إذا حميت

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud said the stones are sulfur stones God created in the lowest heaven when He created the heavens and earth, preparing them for disbelievers; Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who graded the report to the standards of al-Bukhari and Muslim.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن مسعود، في قوله تعالى: {وقودها الناس والحجارة} قال: هي حجارة من كبريت، خلقها الله يوم خلق السماوات والأرض

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi, reporting from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Masud, and other Companions, says the stones are black sulfur stones in Hell used to torment its inhabitants alongside the fire.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي في تفسيره، عن أبي مالك، وعن أبي صالح، عن ابن عباس، وعن مرة عن ابن مسعود، وعن ناس من الصحابة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the stones are sulfur stones more foul-smelling than carrion.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: حجارة من كبريت أنتن من الجيفة.

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر محمد بن علي
rows.claim: Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali also identifies the stones as sulfur stones.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو جعفر محمد بن علي: [هي] (8) حجارة من كبريت.

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj specifies that they are black sulfur stones in the fire.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: حجارة من كبريت أسود في النار

rows.speaker: عمرو بن دينار
rows.claim: Amr ibn Dinar says the sulfur stones are harder and larger than ordinary stones.
rows.anchor: وقال لي عمرو بن دينار: أصلب من هذه الحجارة وأعظم

rows.speaker: فخر الدين
rows.claim: Fakhr al-Din reports and prefers the view that the stones are idols worshipped apart from God, rather than sulfur fuel stones; Ibn Kathir rejects this preference as weak.
rows.anchor: حكاه القرطبي وفخر الدين ورجحه على الأول؛ قال: لأن أخذ النار في حجارة الكبريت ليس بمنكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says the idol interpretation is weak: sulfur stones intensify the fire, fire heating stones is observable, and the verse emphasizes the promised fire’s heat and blazing force.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي قاله ليس بقوي،؛ وذلك أن النار إذا أضرمت بحجارة الكبريت كان ذلك أشد لحرها وأقوى لسعيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir cites 17:97 to show how the fire’s intensity is increased whenever it subsides; al-Qurtubi likewise prefers stones that fuel and intensify the blaze because that makes the torment worse.
rows.anchor: كما قال: {كلما خبت زدناهم سعيرا} [الإسراء: 97] . وهكذا رجح القرطبي أن المراد بها الحجارة التي تسعر بها النار

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi cites a report that every harmful thing is in the Fire; Ibn Kathir says the report is not preserved or known.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء في الحديث عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: "كل مؤذ في النار" وهذا الحديث ليس بمحفوظ ولا معروف

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi gives two readings of the harmful-things report: everyone who harms people enters the Fire, or harmful creatures inhabit it and torment its people.
rows.anchor: ثم قال القرطبي: وقد فسر بمعنيين، أحدهما: أن كل من آذى الناس دخل النار (2) ، والآخر: كل ما يؤذي فهو في النار يتأذى به أهلها
